http://www.europesun.com/news/279205984/.text: EU caves in on new Russia sanctions - media RT.com 23 Jul 2026, 17:30 GMT+10 The bloc has been forced to approve a watered-down package, including a Greek-backed exemption that allows EU companies to transport Russian LNG The EU has relented on objections from member states, granting what one diplomat has described as an "outrageous exemption," to issue a watered-down sanctions package targeting Russia. Greece successfully lobbied to allow EU companies to continue transporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) to third countries, media reports claimed on Thursday. The package, the EU's 21st since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, was presented by the European Commission in June. It was designed to target Russia's energy, financial, crypto, trade, and fisheries sectors, bar entry to former Russian servicemen, and phase out Russian LNG transportation by EU companies. The bloc held several failed rounds of talks on the package, which requires unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states, with a number of nations arguing that some of the proposals would harm their economic interests. Greece, which has the world's largest independent cross-trade LNG fleet by capacity, warned that banning EU shipping companies from transporting Russian LNG would harm Greek shipping interests, including Dynagas. Dynagas, one of the few European companies that operate ice-class LNG carriers capable of reaching Russia's Yamal LNG project in the Arctic, says its vessels are tied to contracts running until 2065 that predate the Ukraine conflict. It argued that the sanctions could force it to sell its fleet, weakening Europe's shipping industry while benefiting foreign competitors. Greece also reportedly warned that the measure could trigger widespread reflagging to jurisdictions where EU rules would be harder to enforce, and pushed for an indefinite exemption. According to Euractiv and Euronews, citing diplomats, under a compromise brokered by the EU's rotating presidency which is held by Ireland, ambassadors signed off on the package on Thursday after agreeing to a renewable 12-month waiver allowing the Greek company and other EU companies to continue transporting Russian LNG, subject to annual reviews. They also approved a 12-month freeze on adjustments to the G7's $44.10-per-barrel price cap on Russian oil. Without the move, the cap would have automatically increased on Thursday under a mechanism linked to global oil prices, which Brussels reportedly opposed as it would have raised the ceiling to $58 per barrel, benefiting Russia. Watered-down deal Apart from the Greek concession, the final package is reportedly significantly diluted. A Baltic-backed proposal to ban Russians who served in the military after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict from entering the bloc was scaled back after France, Italy , and Greece pushed back. The measure now only applies to short-stay visas and narrows the criteria from general military service to direct participation in military operations. EU envoys also reportedly dropped plans to phase out Russian fish imports following resistance from Germany, Poland, and Portugal, which sought to protect domestic processors. Efforts to sanction Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, were also reportedly blocked after opposition from Bulgaria and Italy, ensuring his removal from the blacklist. The package, however, reportedly blacklists around 250 individuals and entities accused of supporting Russia's military operation against Ukraine, "spreading propaganda," or helping circumvent sanctions, as well as more than 600 vessels linked to the supposed 'shadow fleet', which allegedly helps Russia bypass sanctions on oil exports. It also targets Russian banks, crypto platforms, and oil traders. The final version of the package must still undergo technical revisions before being adopted by all 27 member states. Behind Brussels' 'united front' Analysts and diplomats say the long-debated package highlights growing divisions within the bloc as the sanctions increasingly clash with member states' economic interests. "There's no more low-hanging fruit, with 20 packages done," one EU diplomat told Politico. Some say the standoff exposes the fact that there was never actual unanimity on sanctions, and that former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban's departure has deprived other EU capitals of a convenient shield. For years, the scapegoating of Orban allowed other governments to hide behind Budapest while defending their own economic interests. With Peter Magyar now in office and Hungary no longer blocking the sanctions, the objections have openly surfaced. "It has been a surprise and a disappointment how many member states have stalled in their actions," Finnish MEP Ville Niinisto told Politico. Another diplomat said: "Orban was difficult, but he never actually blocked whole packages." READ MORE: Orban's exit through global eyes: Who really gains - and who doesn't The package comes as the EU continues to face soaring energy costs after slashing most Russian energy imports following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, and according to consultancy Wood Mackenzie, risks entering the upcoming heating season with its lowest gas reserves in 15 years. The bloc still imports Russian LNG, which accounts for around 14% of its supplies, even as Brussels prepares to ban purchases from January 1. The EU imported a record 9.89 million tons of LNG from Russia's Yamal project in the first half of 2026, the Financial Times reported earlier this week. Moscow has long maintained that the sanctions will not alter its political course or have a decisive impact on its economy, while analysts have warned that the sanctions largely backfire on those that impose them. https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: CLACTON-ON-SEA — Voters seeking to re-elect Nigel Farage Thursday will have to scan past an array of comedy characters and oddballs on the longest ballot paper in British history. The man who hopes to be the U.K.’s next prime minister is all but certain to retain his seaside fiefdom of Clacton — but his self-styled “people versus the establishment” electoral gambit is sowing some seeds of discontent even among loyal supporters. Fear of Clacton becoming a “laughing stock” is a common refrain during a pair of focus groups POLITICO attended in the run-up to this week’s election. Advertisement Advertisement The feeling that the town has been made to look daft was apparent even among those preparing to vote once again to return the Reform UK leader to parliament. And it’s not the rival candidate wearing a trash can on his head that they’re holding responsible for the “farce.” Thursday may not be the end of the matter, either. A parliamentary investigation into Farage’s alleged failure to declare millions of pounds of donations in the run-up to his 2024 election could mean yet another by-election — and a tougher battle for the right-wing populist next time around. Bid for absolution This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents. Ordinary punters, he argued, should be the ones to have their say as he faced mounting questions over undeclared donations. The gamble was that such a vote would absolve him of wrongdoing in the eyes of the public, regardless of the findings in two parliamentary probes — one over a £5 million donation from a crypto-entrepreneur, and the other into support from a convicted fraudster. Farage has denied wrongdoing in both instances, arguing that help was given in a personal capacity. Reform UK Party Leader Nigel Farage gestures as he speaks during a press conference on a plan to deport foreign prisoners on August 10, 2026 at Royal Horseguards Hotel in London. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images But Britain’s main political parties took one look at this ploy and opted out. That’s how Count Binface, one of the most enthusiastic inheritors of a rich British tradition of standing as a satirical candidate in elections, ended up as Farage’s most high-profile rival. Others risking their £500 deposit to get their names on the 90-cm-long ballot paper include rival jokesters with names ranging from Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap. Broadcast rules mean the 34-strong candidate list needs to be read in full at every mention of Farage’s by-election on TV. Advertisement Advertisement A seaside town back on the map — in ways unwanted The first focus group arranged by the More in Common think tank that POLITICO observed was made up of 12 constituents who all voted for Farage in the 2024 general election, and are minded to do so again in the by-election. (Their names were withheld so they could speak candidly). It was a retiree who was first to volunteer regret at Farage’s decision, blaming him for provoking an “influx of idiots” into the constituency. “Unfortunately, the action of causing a by-election has,” the former shopkeeper offered, “really made Clacton, in my opinion, a bit of a laughing stock.” Two others repeated that same phrase, with one dog groomer-by-trade adding: “I think it was all a bit of a farce. I think he should have admitted that he was given this £5 million.” “I guess it makes it very hard to trust him,” a delivery driver chimed in. “Most of my friends have gone towards Count Binface as opposed to Farage.” Count Binface of the Count Binface Party speaks to the media at the By-election declaration at The Edge where votes were being counted on June 19, 2026 in Wigan. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images Farage has since given varying explanations for some of the money he’s received, including as a “reward” for Brexit, or to cover lifelong security in the perilous world of modern politics. The veteran campaigner has been tetchy about the “unconditional gift” during media appearances, telling a radio interviewer he could spend it on Ferraris or bet on the horses, adding: “What’s it got to do with you?” The dog groomer was among those lamenting the cost of running the by-election too. Reform had offered to pay for it, but in reality there is no mechanism to do this. The sheer number of candidates running has some extraordinary consequences. Advertisement Advertisement Tendring Council, which is presiding over the vote, said even the cost of printing the ballot papers is four times that of a typical election because of their sheer length. Additional planning has had to go into every stage, from how the ballot is printed, folded and actually cast at polling stations — and counting will go on through the night and possibly past breakfast. Then there are the Reform voters who have now been forced to choose whether to cast a vote for a comedy candidate or for Farage. “From what I can tell about Binface, he seems like an okay guy from the research I’ve done,” said one local businessman. “And I do think there would be some tourism involved because of the absurdity of having that candidate as the MP of Clacton.” This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images That influx could already be observed, to some extent, on Tuesday this week. Even though it’s a school holiday, the pier and the amusement arcades in town weren’t exactly heaving with holiday-makers. But there was a steady stream of journalists — so many that they even tried to vox pop each other at times. Then there was an obscure mobile phone network that set up an ice cream van selling “99s for 99p” — in a publicity stunt echoing one of Binface’s manifesto pledges. A vintage Jaguar painted all over with the Union Jack (and used in the Austin Powers franchise ) is touring the streets all day in support of Binface. Farage’s social media has done a good job of showing how much support he still commands from the diehards — at times at messiah-like levels . And it’s not hard to find his “I’m with Nigel” placards outside homes, a picture of the candidate ringed with a halo-like ferris wheel. Advertisement Advertisement But supporters in the first focus group suggested that the sheen could be coming off a man who has, just this year, been enough of a campaigning force to send the governing Labour Party searching for a new leader. Old-school Tories’ views harden The second focus group, held in a community garden overlooking the town, featured right-wing voters, and comprised largely of former Conservative supporters who, though discontented with their old party, aren’t eager to back Farage any time soon. They roundly agreed with the “farce” analysis of the by-election. “People see this by-election as a total joke. If you talk to anyone, then that is their view,” said a retired printer. They all lamented having no proper choice, though they generally backed the decision by Farage’s mainstream rivals not to contest the vote. A poster that reads ‘Clacton Fear’ is seen on Clacton Pier on August 06, 2026 in Clacton-on-Sea. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images One bridge player with a firm grasp on politics described playing “eeny, meeny, miny, moe” with her postal vote to randomly pick a candidate who wasn’t Farage. Another spoke of spoiling her postal ballot and writing that the whole affair is a waste of time and money. These were all the kind of right-wingers who Farage would want to win over to elevate himself from an insurgent outsider to true contender for high office — but their stances only seemed to have hardened in response to the by-election. Advertisement Advertisement Anything but a crushing Farage victory would be a major upset. Constituency polling has him on course to win 73 percent of the vote to Binface’s 20 percent. Turnout in this bizarre by-election will also be closely looked at, as will spoiled ballots. Reform aides have already been planning a victory speech to take place after the votes have finally been counted on Friday. But first their candidate will have to undergo that British ritual of standing next to an array of comedy characters on a stage in a leisure center to hear the results. Should Farage make it back to parliament as expected, then the standards commissioner’s investigation into the donations resumes. That means yet more scrutiny at a time when Labour is riding a polling bounce after Andy Burnham took over as prime minister. For the first time since March last year, Labour has topped POLITICO’s poll of polls ahead of Reform. The government’s apparent rehabilitation — combined with Reform being squeezed on the right by the splinter Restore Britain party — is adding to a worsening picture for Farage. If the Reform UK leader is found to have committed wrongdoing and ends up being suspended from parliament, the next by-election — should he choose to fight it — could pose a far greater challenge. Not only would he come up against real opposition, but voters will have read yet more headlines about mega-bucks donations as they’re forced to the polls once again. “It’ll be bad for us and it’ll make us look even more stupid,” said a Reform-minded instrument salesman when asked about the prospect of another by-election. “But then he [Farage] was the one that called it.” Advertisement

Sobyanin did not report any damage or casualties, though said that emergency responders had been deployed to the site of fallen debris. Advertisement Advertisement Moscow's regional Gov. Ukraine scales up drone attacks in Moscow, across Russia to record highs, data shows Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed at least 822 Ukrainian drones overnight. The craft were shot down over 16 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. Local officials reported that five people were killed by a drone attack in the Rostov region and that one person was killed in a drone attack on a bus in the Belgorod region. Ukraine's air force said Russian forces launched several missiles and 106 drones into the country in its latest barrage, of which three missiles and 85 drones were shot down or otherwise suppressed. Impacts of Russian munitions were reported across 13 locations, the air force said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to Telegram that at least six people were injured in the capital Kyiv and across the surrounding region. Two people were killed by Russian strikes in Zelenskyy's home city of Kryvyi Rih, the president wrote, as was one person in the northeastern city of Sumy. Amid Russia's latest barrage, at least one drone was reported as having crossed into NATO airspace in Romania, from the direction of Moldova. https://www.dw.com/en/why-north-korea-s-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MQmc Kim's dismissive stance toward Trump reflects North Korea's growing confidence that it no longer needs a grand bargain with the US [FILE: June 30, 2019] Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP Advertisement Last month, US President Donald Trump revived a charm offensive aimed at Pyongyang by drastically scaling back joint US military exercises with South Korea and pouring praise on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The US president said the North Korean dictator "has always treated me with great respect." North Korea's response to Trump's overtures has been markedly less enthusiastic, ranging from firing a barrage of missiles to publicly denying Trump's claims that Kim has responded "very positively" to a request for talks. This week, as the US and South Korea, along with Japan, kicked off a five-day military drill, there was no mention of any pullback from Washington, nor any sign of diplomatic progress with Pyongyang. Instead, Kim on Monday commissioned a naval destroyer, while again emphasizing North Korea must establish a "powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent" and strengthen "maritime defense." Kim also said North Korea would soon unveil a "significant" naval advancement. Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video No urgency for deal with US Unlike the summit diplomacy of Trump's first term, Kim's dismissive stance comes at a time when North Korea has alternatives to a grand bargain with the United States. "For Kim, the stakes are simply lower than they were in 2019. There is no longer the same sense of urgency in Pyongyang to get back to the negotiating table with Washington," Joon Ha Park, a correspondent at Korea Risk Group in Seoul, told DW. "North Korea now has a treaty-based alliance with Moscow and is drawing closer to Beijing, while its military capabilities have expanded significantly. That's why a single reduction in ROK-US military exercises is not enough for Pyongyang to be swayed," he added, referring to military ties between South Korea and the US. Kim rides high Park agrees that Kim is arguably in his strongest position since taking power in 2011. Just six years ago, amid crippling sanctions and the coronavirus pandemic, an emotional Kim stood at the lectern marking the 75th anniversary of the Korean Workers' Party and expressed regret for having failed the North Korean people. Fast forward to today, and North Korea's economy appears to be on a stronger footing . Estimates released last year by South Korea's central bank showed the economy expanded by 3.7% in 2024, its fastest rate of growth in eight years. South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Kim has brought North Korea closer to Russia and China than the traditionally isolated country has been in decades. This week, both Moscow and Beijing sent messages marking North Korea's 78th founding anniversary and praising the strategic importance of their deepening partnerships with Pyongyang. Kim's recent spate of good fortune began in 2023 after a summit with Vladimir Putin in Russia's far east. The meeting opened the door for North Korea delivering arms to help Russia fight the Ukraine war, with Moscow sending back aid. Since then, Pyongyang has heavily ramped up industrial military production, buoyed by fresh financing that skirts international sanctions. Beijing responds to the Russia-North Korea alliance China, North Korea's traditional benefactor, quickly took notice of the growing alignment between Moscow and Pyongyang, but initially kept its distance. "The war in Ukraine has opened up a crucial lifeline for the (North Korean) regime, delivering weapons, ammunitions and soldiers to Russia in return for cash, foodstuff and ostensibly advanced military technology," Alexander Lipke, policy fellow with the Asia Program at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW. "These warming ties with Russia have also alarmed China, which is also actively attempting to cement its position as Pyongyang's preeminent partner," he added. By 2025, Russia and North Korea's ever closer ties forced Beijing to pivot and showcase its leading role among the three countries . In September that year, Kim was invited to the "Victory Day" celebrations in Beijing, and for the first time, stood publicly on stage alongside Xi and Putin. For a regime known for its international isolation, Kim standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of Russia and China was a major milestone. This was again the case when in June 2026, Xi's first foreign trip of the year took him to Pyongyang. Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Denuclearization off the table? Notably, any mention of "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" was omitted from communiques following these high-level meetings, despite the phrase previously being part of boilerplate diplomatic language from Beijing and Moscow. This diplomatic softening comes as North Korea aggressively takes steps to ramp up its nuclear program. In February 2026, Kim said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "irreversible," while calling for the country's nuclear force to be expanded. Recent analysis of satellite imagery suggests increased activity at known North Korean nuclear sites. Pyongyang has also insisted on US recognition as a nuclear weapons state as a precondition for any talks with Washington, while emphasizing that any future summits must omit language on "denuclearization." North Korea is estimated to have nearly 60 nuclear warheads, which is double the 20-30 warheads Pyongyang is thought to have possessed during Trump's last diplomatic episode with Kim in 2018 and 2019. "North Korea is no longer looking for talks centered on denuclearization or even traditional arms control. It increasingly wants recognition, implicitly or otherwise, as a nuclear weapons state," said Park from the Korea Risk Group. He added that any Trump summit without denuclearization included as part of the official agenda "could be portrayed by Pyongyang both domestically and internationally as implicit US acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status." What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Sanctions don't matter anymore? Since its first nuclear test in 2006, North Korea has been subject to a strict sanctions regime, with the UN Security Council having passed nine sanctions resolutions aimed at restricting exports, along with asset freezes. The last package was passed in 2017. At that point, it was combined with pressure and fiery rhetoric from the first Trump administration, raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula. Kim was under heavy economic pressure and seeking sanctions relief in return for concessions on his nuclear program. But that moment has now long passed. "North Korea's diplomatic situation has vastly improved, reducing the pressure to come to the table to cut a deal with the US," said Lipke, adding that "independent sanctions enforcement has widely collapsed," with Russia and China no longer actively pursuing their non-proliferation stance of previous decades. Lipke said North Korea no longer needs a bargain with the US regarding sanctions relief in return for partial denuclearization. "But the bargain now on the table could potentially be much larger for North Korea, a freeze in nuclear development in exchange for the recognition by the US as a de-facto nuclear state in front of the whole world."
